source: Bilalic, Graf, Vaci, Danek (2019) The temporal dynamics of insight problem solving: restructuring might not always be sudden
finding: Eye tracking on matchstick arithmetic. On the group average, attention to the crucial element (the plus sign) rose slowly before the solution, which looks gradual. Individual traces were mixed. Solvers who shifted attention earlier rated the solution as less sudden and less surprising.
numbers: Individual level: 27% of solvers showed a sudden looking pattern, 54% an incremental pattern. 73 participants on easy Problem A, about 61 on hard Problem B; 34% solved B unaided (as reported in the Graf et al. 2023 re-analysis).
quote: restructuring might not always be sudden
limits: One problem family, one measure (gaze). Group averaging can hide sudden shifts; the 2023 follow-up (b02) warns the ANOVA used here was the wrong tool.
agent_relevance: Restructuring can be a ramp, not a jump. The agent should not assume a single flip; track gradual evidence toward a new framing and allow an explicit switch when it crosses a threshold.

source: Graf, Vaci, Bilalic, Danek et al. (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: using GAMs and change point analysis to uncover restructuring
finding: Re-analysis of the 2019 eye data. Classical ANOVA cannot detect an abrupt shift. Generalised additive models and change-point models find an abrupt attention shift to the crucial element around the 90% point of the solving period in solvers. Hints changed the dynamics in a different, more reorienting way.
numbers: The sudden-pattern figure in the paper uses SIMULATED data (footnote 2); the real Bilalic 2019 data indicate a gradual shift. Only 34% solved unaided; an extra 11% solved after the hint.
limits: Methods paper. The suddenness verdict depends on the statistical model chosen, so neither side gets clean support from this data.
agent_relevance: The suddenness debate is partly a measurement debate. When testing whether a restructure operator flipped, use change-point style checks, not averages over runs.

source: Danek and Wiley (2017) What about false insights? Deconstructing the Aha! experience along its multiple dimensions for correct and incorrect solutions
finding: With 37 magic tricks, Aha ratings were higher for correct than for incorrect solutions, but many wrong answers also felt like an Aha (false insights). Pleasure, suddenness and certainty were the main parts of the Aha. Correct solutions felt relieved, incorrect ones felt surprising.
numbers: N=70. Aha rating correct M=66.5 (SD 18.4) vs incorrect M=52.3 (SD 18.8), t(69)=10.21. 37% (417 of 1124) of incorrect solutions got an Aha rating above the correct-solution average. Correct solutions were faster: 35.8 s vs 42.5 s. Solvers were 23% overconfident on tricks they solved wrongly.
limits: No feedback given. Magic tricks are not classic insight problems. Many wrong solutions were partial.
agent_relevance: A felt sense of it clicked is a weak signal of being right. A sudden-feeling answer still needs a verification step; confidence must not replace testing.

source: Webb, Little, Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types
finding: Three experiments with classic insight problems, compound remote associates (CRAs) and non-insight problems, with continuous Aha ratings. Insight problems got higher insight ratings than non-insight problems. Correct solutions got stronger Aha than incorrect ones. Aha was linked to accuracy for insight problems and CRAs, and much less for non-insight problems.
numbers: Aha-accuracy correlations in Exp 1: classic insight r=0.50 (BF10>150), CRAs r=0.41 (BF10>150), non-insight r=0.02 (BF10<1). Exp 1a: insight r=0.40, CRAs r=0.40, non-insight r=0.24 (p=0.04). Exp 2 (with feedback): insight r=0.495, CRAs r=0.39, non-insight r=0.19. Insight minus non-insight rating difference about 6 points (BF10 about 76) in Exp 1a.
limits: ESL participants were filtered after Exp 1 because of low CRA accuracy. Insight is a property of the solver experience, not the problem, as the title says.
agent_relevance: Treat insight as a solver state, not a task type. Key the scaffold on observable impasse and representation-change signals, not on problem category.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden, Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
finding: Across four experiments (anagrams, visual rebus-type, mixed problems) self-labelled insight solutions were more accurate than analytic ones. Analytic errors were more often errors of commission (a wrong guess), insight errors more often omissions (timeouts).
numbers: Insight vs analytic accuracy: Exp 1 d=0.99 (t(37)=5.66, p<.001), narrower window d=0.74; Exp 2 d=1.50 and 0.51 (t(50)); a later experiment d=0.66 and 0.39 (t(109)); another d=1.85 and 1.24 (t(26)). Analytic-labelled errors exceeded insight-labelled errors, d about -0.4 to -1.85.
limits: Self-report labels, no feedback. Only partly consistent with b03: insight is on average more accurate yet not perfect.
agent_relevance: All-or-nothing arrival is a mild accuracy signal; premature stops give wrong guesses. Answers produced after a hard stop on partial search deserve lower trust than ones that arrive when search is complete.

source: Schoenauer, Brodt, Pohlchen, Bressmer, Danek, Gais (2018) Sleep does not promote solving classical insight problems and magic tricks
finding: No benefit of sleep or incubation on insight problems or magic tricks, and no change in the number of solutions reported with insight.
numbers: N=77 in a 3-hour sleep vs wake by incubation vs none design. Magic tricks: incubation F(1,64)=0.008, p=0.93; sleep F(1,64)=0.047, p=0.83. Initial phase solved 2.66 (SE 0.21) of 10 tricks; 1.40 (SE 0.13) more at retest. Initial solve rates for matchstick, nine-dot, eight-coin: 45.5%, 6.0%, 8.0%. Insight reported for 66% of matchstick, 42% of nine-dot and 47% of eight-coin solutions.
limits: Single 3-hour window. Consistent with the failed-incubation literature, not a refutation of every incubation benefit.
agent_relevance: No evidence that rest alone restructures. A pause with no new input should not be expected to help; spend effort on operators that change the representation.

source: Salmon-Mordekovich and Leikin (2023) Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite as usual
finding: Tested special-process vs business-as-usual with four problem types and dual tasks (inner speech suppression, spatial tapping). Verbal insight problems differed from verbal non-insight, but resembled spatial non-insight problems. Neither insight nor spatial non-insight solving was hurt by the secondary tasks. Analogical and convergent thinking predicted both.
numbers: 88.5% of correctly solved insight problems were reported as insight, yet only 7.97% of those included an impasse. Impasse reported while silently solving: 1.7% of participants on verbal non-insight, 37% verbal insight, 41% spatial insight, 21% spatial non-insight. Regressions explained 32%, 37% and 34% of variance for verbal insight, spatial insight, spatial non-insight.
limits: Individual-differences design, moderate N. Authors endorse an unequally integrated mix of both theories.
agent_relevance: Supports mostly ordinary processing plus occasional special moves. Restructuring can be an ordinary operator driven by analogy and convergent search, not a magic jump.

source: Macchi, Poli, Caravona (2025) Dissociable effects of verbalization on solving insight and non-insight problems
finding: Concurrent verbalisation hurt the insight problem (Deer problem) and greatly helped the non-insight problem (revised cryptarithmetic). Replicates Macchi and Bagassi (2012) with a new problem and favours an unconscious analytic thought view over business-as-usual.
numbers: Solved with silence vs verbalising: insight problem 57% vs 13%; non-insight problem 30% vs 80%. A Cox hazards model with a problem type by verbalisation interaction was significant.
limits: Small between-subject cells. Other studies (Gilhooly; Fleck and Weisberg) found no verbal overshadowing, so results are mixed across problems and analyses.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: forced step-by-step talk helps procedural tasks but can harm tasks that need a reinterpretation. Test whether forced verbose chain-of-thought hurts reframing items.

source: Macchi, Inglese, Caravona (2026) Does physical interaction with insight problems really affect the solution rate?
finding: Handling real pencils did not help on a spatial insight problem. A picture of real matchsticks, which shows that operators can be decomposed, raised matchstick arithmetic solves. Help comes from clearing a misunderstanding, not from manipulation itself.
numbers: Pencil problem: 27.3% (12/44) paper vs 32.6% (14/43) interactive, chi2(1,N=87)=0.290, p=.590. STEM students 46.7% (21/45) vs non-STEM 11.9% (5/42). Matchstick arithmetic: 46.7% (14/30) standard vs 79.3% (23/29) matchstick picture, chi2(1,N=59)=6.720, p=.010, V=0.337.
limits: Small samples, student populations, one-off problems.
agent_relevance: Interventions that change the representation (a better depiction) beat ones that add activity. Operator: re-draw or re-encode the problem in a different form.

source: Becker, Wang, Cabeza (2024) Surprise! Clarifying the link between insight and prediction error
finding: Preregistered online study with verbal insight problems (CRAs). Aha tracked a metacognitive prediction error about solvability. Of the Aha parts, surprise tracked the prediction error; pleasure, certainty and suddenness did not, and suddenness correlated negatively with it.
numbers: Direction of effects from the abstract and text; exact coefficients not extracted this session.
limits: CRAs are the weakest proxy for Gestalt insight. Online sample.
agent_relevance: Insight may be a prediction error on expected solve time. A monitor that compares expected and actual progress is a cleaner trigger than a vague click.

source: Cushen and Wiley (2012) Cues to solution, restructuring patterns, and reports of insight in creative problem solving (via Bilalic et al. 2019)
finding: Individual-level importance ratings of problem elements showed both sudden and incremental restructuring. Reports of insight did not map well onto the actual pattern.
numbers: Sudden pattern 68% of cases, incremental 32% (Triangle of Circles problem), as cited in Bilalic et al.
limits: Second-hand: read only through the Bilalic text, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as b01: restructuring dynamics vary by solver and the felt Aha is a poor readout of them.

source: Danek, Williams, Wiley (2018) Closing the gap: connecting sudden representational change to the Aha! experience (via Bilalic et al. 2019)
finding: 18 magic tricks, element importance ratings over three viewings. Few solutions showed a sudden representational change.
numbers: 14% of correct solutions sudden pattern, 10% incremental, the rest flat, decreasing or zigzag, as cited in Bilalic et al.
limits: Second-hand citation.
agent_relevance: Most solves show neither a clean jump nor a clean ramp; do not overfit an operator to one shape.

source: Durso, Rea, Dayton (1994) Graph-theoretic confirmation of restructuring during insight (via Bilalic et al. 2019)
finding: Solution-relevant word pairs were rated as more related as solvers approached the answer, on group averages.
numbers: Bilalic quotes Durso: the insightful solution explodes with breathtaking suddenness, but a long fuse warns of it.
limits: Averaged data and repeated ratings may have cued participants (Bilalic critique). Smith and Kounios (1996) did not replicate gradual accumulation in anagrams.
agent_relevance: Early evidence for a gradual build-up behind a sudden-feeling answer; argues for tracking latent progress.

source: Novick and Sherman (2003) On the nature of insight solutions: evidence from skill differences in anagram solution (via Bilalic et al. 2019)
finding: Solvers discriminated solvable from unsolvable anagrams within 250 ms, increasingly well with presentation time, read as gradual accumulation of information.
numbers: Exact accuracies not read this session.
limits: Second-hand; solutions were given right after the judgments, so the actual finding of a solution was not measured.
agent_relevance: Fast partial signals exist before an answer is found. Use cheap solvability probes before committing compute.

source: Ohlsson (1992/2011) Information-processing explanations of insight (as quoted in Bilalic 2019 and Danek and Wiley 2017)
finding: Representational change theory: restructuring by constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition and re-encoding after an impasse. The apparent suddenness of the full solution may be an illusion of limited introspection, and perceived suddenness depends on how many steps remain after the key change.
numbers: No data. Danek and Wiley (2017) test the steps-remaining idea in their trick set.
quote: the sudden appearance of the complete solution in consciousness is an illusion
limits: Theory claim. Ohlsson himself allowed erroneous insights (1984b).
agent_relevance: Defines the operator: relax a constraint, decompose a chunk, re-encode. Suddenness of the output is not a design target.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (from memory; not opened)
finding: Meta-analysis of incubation studies: small positive overall effect, larger for divergent-thinking than insight problems, larger with low-demand tasks in the break.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 117 effect sizes, small overall effect.
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified. Later work (b06) finds no sleep or incubation boost.
agent_relevance: Weak, conditional support for breaks. Only worth building in as a cheap option.

source: Schooler, Ohlsson, Brooks (1993) Thoughts beyond words: when language overshadows insight (from memory; not opened)
finding: Talking aloud while solving reduced insight problem performance but not non-insight performance. Origin of the verbal overshadowing claim tested in b08.
numbers: From memory, unverified: large drop in insight solve rate under verbalisation.
limits: Not opened. Replication is mixed (see b08 on Gilhooly and Fleck and Weisberg null results).
agent_relevance: Same as b08.

source: Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) Intuition in insight and noninsight problem solving (via Danek and Wiley 2017)
finding: Feeling-of-warmth ratings rose gradually for non-insight problems but jumped just before the answer for insight problems, taken as evidence for sudden insight.
numbers: Danek and Wiley cite Metcalfe (1986b): 76% of correct solutions came after a sudden warmth jump, but 52% of incorrect solutions also showed a sudden jump.
limits: Second-hand. Warmth ratings are themselves an interrupting subjective measure.
agent_relevance: Warmth is the classic progress monitor. A sudden jump in felt closeness is not proof the answer is correct.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Aha Moment Revisited: are VLMs truly capable of self verification in inference-time scaling?
finding: In RL-tuned vision-language models, a-ha style self-correction is rare and does not reliably raise accuracy. Majority voting beat best-of-N with self-verification.
numbers: A-ha moments in 8.3% of responses (fewer than 10% overall); correction probability low. One reported comparison: majority vote 65.5 vs CoT 49.5. Verifier sometimes did better with the image removed (changes up to 16.7%). Models: Qwen2-VL-2B, R1-VL, VLAA-Thinker, VL-Rethinker; data GeoQA170K, MathVista.
limits: Visual math only; small open models.
agent_relevance: Sudden mid-trace wait reversals are not a dependable source of gains. Prefer sampling plus voting and external verification over trusting an in-trace restructure.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-like training: a critical perspective
finding: The R1-Zero aha moment is not created by RL. Base models including DeepSeek-V3-Base already produce reflection phrases such as Aha and wait. More self-reflection in R1-Zero did not go with higher accuracy.
numbers: 500 MATH questions with the R1 template on DeepSeek-V3-Base-685B. Reflection keywords appear in base output; R1-Zero reflects more often but reflection is not positively correlated with accuracy.
limits: Keyword counting is crude (the authors add an LLM check). Math only.
agent_relevance: The LLM aha is mostly surface text. Do not count it as proof of representational change; check whether the framing actually changed.

source: Hu et al. (2025) Beyond Aha!: toward systematic meta-abilities alignment in large reasoning models
finding: Rather than wait for an emergent aha, train deduction, induction and abduction as separate meta-abilities, then merge. Aggregated models lift accuracy by more than 10% over an instruction-tuned baseline.
numbers: 7B: induction-aligned model raised the mean score by 1.7 points (from 38.8%); 32B: mean gain 3.1% on Math-overall and 2.6% overall.
limits: A training method, not a scaffold; authors' own benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Argues for explicit, composable reasoning moves over reliance on emergent insight. Fits an operator-list approach.

source: Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi, Taati (2023) Large language models are fixated by red herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: LLMs show an Einstellung-like fixation: puzzles with deliberate red herrings are far harder than versions with red herrings removed. More few-shot examples barely helped.
numbers: Test set 494 walls. GPT-4 10-shot solved 6 walls on original OCW, 59 on OCW-Randomized, 471 on OCW-WordNet; correct groups 239, 595, 1926. GPT-3.5-turbo 10-shot: 0, 10, 415 solved walls. Human about 80% of connections vs best model 41-45% F1.
limits: Table read from a jumbled PDF layout; the 6/59/471 reading follows row order. Quiz-show data may sit in training sets.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of fixation on a wrong representation. A scaffold needs a drop-the-obvious-grouping operator and a check for decoy structure.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: lateral thinking puzzles for large language models
finding: Lateral thinking puzzles that need breaking default commonsense. Models fall far below humans, and drop further on semantically or contextually reconstructed versions, which suggests memorisation.
numbers: Strongest model ChatGPT 53% and 63% on the two subtasks vs random 25% and human 92% (102 questions, three experts).
limits: Multiple choice; 2023 models only.
agent_relevance: A testbed for reframing. Reconstruction checks guard against memorised answers.

source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) CresOWLve: benchmarking creative problem-solving over real-world knowledge
finding: Frontier LLMs, including thinking models, do worse on creative connection questions than on factual versions of the same knowledge. They retrieve the facts but fail to link them in a non-obvious way.
numbers: 2,061 examples across five difficulty levels. Creative minus factual drop from -6.08% (Gemini-3.1-Pro high) to -17.21% (Mistral-Large-3-675B-Instruct) on the English set; smaller on the Russian set (about -2% to -3% for Gemini). Even the best thinking models lose more than 20% accuracy from very simple to very hard.
limits: Puzzles from a Russian intellectual game; contamination risk acknowledged; no human baseline.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is the connection step, not recall. An operator that deliberately pairs retrieved facts under new framings targets that gap.

source: Graf et al. 2023 / Bilalic 2019: hint effects on restructuring
finding: Explicit hints sharply redirected attention to the crucial element, yet did not guarantee a solution: solvers still spent long trying variants and non-solvers returned to the old focus.
numbers: After the hint an additional 11% solved (34% unaided).
limits: Single problem.
agent_relevance: A correct hint is not enough. Allow search time after reframing; do not stop at the first revised framing.
